প্রবন্ধ ও সাহিত্যসমালোচনা

AI in World Literature: Authorship, Ownership, and Literature’s New Crisis

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-11-21

About six months ago, a young writer posted a story in a literary group on Facebook. Along with it came a candid announcement: “The story was written with AI. It took ten minutes.” The story was six hundred words long. There were no spelling mistakes, the sentences were smooth, there was rain at the beginning and a twist at the end. Reading it felt like eating a curry at a hotel. You feel full, but the taste does not stay with you. The most unsettling thing was that there was no sense of a human presence in the story. The writer was nowhere to be felt; there was only a pile of beautiful sentences.

Out of curiosity, I tried the same thing myself. I asked: “Write a six-hundred-word story about a river in a village.” The story arrived in three and a half seconds. There was a river, a boat, a fisherman, even the evening light was there in just the right way. But the river I know was missing. There was no trace of the river where I once nearly drowned while learning to swim, no trace of the smell of mud that clung to my body until evening. The machine has read books about rivers, but it has never seen a river. That difference is the heart of the matter.

What is literature made of? Words—the answer is simple, but only half right. The other half is made of the life behind the writing. Staying awake at night, having manuscripts returned, living through the strain of a household, knowing people at close range—all of these give writing its weight.

The sense of deprivation we find in Manik Bandopadhyay’s stories came from what he saw with his own eyes. AI knows thousands of sentences about poverty, but it has never seen poverty. It can write orderly, polished sentences because it has been built from examples of good writing. Yet readers know that the more neatly arranged a piece of writing becomes, the more its scent often disappears.

So what will happen to original writers? I do not think writers themselves will necessarily be in great danger. The writing market will be. Machine-written texts will be everywhere—in newspaper pages, on Facebook walls, in the inboxes of literary magazines. Yet readers who know literature will still sense which writing carries the scent of a human being. The printing press did not kill handwriting, and the arrival of the typewriter did not stop the pen. The real fear lies somewhere else. New writers are formed through small attempts, rejection, mistakes, and being turned away again and again—the way many of us have stood up only after being rejected day after day. If a machine covers that road, then ten or fifteen years from now the place where familiar writers might have emerged could also be empty. If mature writers are formed through rough, unfinished writing, where will an apprentice writer stand if there is no longer any room for that rough writing?

It is worth looking a little more closely at the printing press, because its history in this country is part of our own history. At the beginning of the nineteenth century, Bengali type was developed and printing began at the Serampore Mission Press, while the Battala market of Calcutta was entering the final days of the handwritten puthi. Even then, many people said angrily that printed books would extinguish the central flame of literature, because the beauty of handwriting would disappear.

The opposite happened. Cheap printed books drew crowds of readers, and from Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar to Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay, one new generation of writers after another began to emerge. Then came the Bengali typewriter, and much later computers and Avro. Each time, people warned of disaster, and each time writing spread further. Yet did anyone lose their affection for handwritten manuscripts? The handwritten pages of writers from those eras are still preserved carefully in museums.

In May 2026, Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir became the Caribbean regional winner of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize with his story “The Serpent in the Grove.” The story had been selected from nearly eight thousand entries. Within days of the announcement, accusations appeared on social media that the story had been written using generative AI. The AI-detection company Pangram identified the story as “100% AI.” Granta publisher Sigrid Rausing then said that they had asked Claude whether the story had been generated by AI. The substance of Claude’s lengthy response was that the story was almost certainly not written by a human. On the basis of that response, Granta ended its long-standing partnership with the Commonwealth Prize.

But in June, the Commonwealth Foundation examined drafts, time-stamped documents, notes, and outlines and cleared the entries. It found no evidence of AI use in the work of any of the five regional winners. On June 30, Nazir was announced as the overall winner of the 2026 prize, worth £5,000. In other words, a machine declared him guilty, while evidence created and examined by humans declared him innocent. No one knows with certainty which judgment was right. But one thing has become clear: the system we are currently using to verify authorship has broken down.

The larger lesson from this incident concerns the limitations of AI-detection technology. These software systems mainly look at certain statistical features of language—the predictability of sentences, repetition of words, and consistency of prose. But a human being can also write extremely smooth and regular prose. If a writer spends a long time editing and refining the language, there is no sound reason to assume that the resulting text was produced by a machine. Writers for whom English is a second language may also deliberately aim for grammatically correct, straightforward sentences, and some characteristics of their writing may overlap with AI-generated prose. A false detection can therefore damage a writer’s reputation, publishing opportunities, and chances of winning a prize.

In the past, when the originality of a piece of writing was questioned, editors or judges would look at the writer’s previous work, manuscripts, and research notes. Now the score produced by a piece of software is also moving to the centre of such disputes. Yet a machine’s calculation of probability is not the same thing as evidence of a human being’s creative labour.

Can readers distinguish between writing produced by a human and writing produced by a machine? A study published in Scientific Reports in November 2024 makes that question even more interesting. Researchers Brian Porter and Edouard Machery conducted an experiment involving 1,634 people. Five poems by writers such as Shakespeare, Byron, Emily Dickinson, T. S. Eliot, Sylvia Plath, and Allen Ginsberg were placed before the participants alongside five poems generated by ChatGPT-3.5 in the styles of those poets. Altogether there were ten poems. Participants correctly identified whether a poem was human-written or machine-generated in only 46.6 percent of cases. More interestingly, readers often gave AI-generated poems high marks for accessibility, rhythm, and beauty, believing them to have been written by humans.

There was reason, however, to be cautious about these findings. The model used was GPT-3.5, much older than the more advanced models available today. Nor were all the participants scholars of poetry. The experiment focused on imitation of familiar poets rather than the creation of entirely new literature. So the study does not show that AI can write better poetry than human beings.

What the study does is place us before a more serious question. How does a reader judge the beauty of a piece of writing? Does making language easy automatically make it good literature? Does a smooth sentence necessarily contain depth? If a reader finds a poem beautiful without knowing who wrote it, does the poem’s literary value change simply because of its origin? I think we need to separate two levels of literary judgment. One is the reader’s experience—what the reader feels while reading the work. The other is the process of creation—how the work came into being, and whose labour, experience, and decisions stand behind it. An AI-generated poem may move or astonish a reader, but that experience of being moved and the question of human authorship are not the same question, and they do not have the same answer.

In March 2026, another incident caused a stir in the international publishing world. British publisher Hachette published American writer Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl in the United Kingdom. Questions about the book’s language and sentence construction spread widely online. Alongside readers’ accusations, an analysis by Pangram claimed that a substantial portion of the book had been generated by a machine. On March 19, Hachette announced that it was cancelling the book’s US publication and halting distribution in the UK. By then, around 1,800 copies had been sold in the United Kingdom. The author denied the allegations. She said that an assistant hired to edit the self-published edition had used AI, but that she herself had not written the novel with AI. Three questions therefore came to the surface at once: the writer’s personal responsibility, the role of the editor, and the publisher’s verification process. The incident matters because a major publishing house changed its commercial decision following the allegations. But it would be wrong to call it proof that the novel “was written by AI.” The writer’s statement and the publisher’s decision are two different things.

This creates a new responsibility for publishers. Should they rely only on a writer’s declaration? Or should they also ask for the history of a manuscript, the stages of editing, and an account of how AI was used? Should a book be withdrawn as soon as an allegation is made? The fact that detection software can also be wrong cannot simply be ignored.

The Commonwealth Prize incident has made this question even deeper. Judges of literary prizes assess more than the beauty of language. They assess imagination, the expression of experience, originality, and literary structure. If authorship itself becomes uncertain, the credibility of the prize also comes into question. Literary institutions therefore cannot simply announce, “AI is banned.” They need to make clear what kinds of use are acceptable, what kinds are not, and how a writer’s contribution will be verified.

To me, the most reliable evidence is the history of the writing process. How did the writer make the first draft? What did they change? How many times did they return to a character or scene? What did their research notes contain? Such evidence can show a continuity of creative labour. I am not arguing that every sentence must be written by hand. But it is possible to provide credible evidence of how a literary work was built. At the same time, it would be wrong to demand that every writer reveal all the contents of their private notebooks or computers. A writer’s privacy and creative freedom matter too. Relevant documents may be requested when necessary for a prize or publication, but writers should not be placed under unnecessary surveillance.

Who owns writing produced with AI? A writer decides the plot, characters, setting, and ending of a novel, but shapes some of its language with the help of AI. Who, then, is the creator of that book? And if an AI company trains its model on thousands of books written by other writers, who is responsible for seeking those writers’ permission or paying them? To answer these questions, we need to separate two issues. The first is the copyright status of writing produced by AI. The second is the legality of using human-written books to train AI systems.

In a report published in January 2025, the US Copyright Office took an important position. According to the Office, writing generated with generative AI may receive copyright protection if a human determines a sufficiently significant part of its expressive content. Simply writing a prompt and asking AI to produce a poem, story, or novel does not automatically turn the output into a human-authored, copyrightable work. But if a person creatively edits or arranges AI-generated material, or incorporates it into original writing in a way that makes the human contribution identifiable, that human contribution may receive protection. Ultimately, the question is where the human creative contribution lies.

One point needs to remain clear here. Copyright and literary value are not the same question. A work does not become good literature merely because it is legally eligible for copyright protection, and a work does not become worthless simply because it receives no copyright protection. The law determines ownership. Literature finds its value through reading, language, aesthetics, and criticism.

One of the major complaints against AI companies is that they are training models on books without the authors’ permission. Several lawsuits have been filed in the United States over this issue. Among them, the case against Anthropic has received particular attention. On July 20, 2026, a federal court in the United States gave final approval to a $1.5 billion settlement in Bartz v. Anthropic. The authors alleged that Anthropic had collected and used copyrighted books without permission to train its Claude model, including books obtained from pirated sources. In the end, the settlement concerned around 482,000 books, with the money going to the writers. But to understand the legal significance of the case, two things need to be kept separate. The court treated the purpose of training and the method by which the materials were acquired as two different questions. The legality of using material for training is one issue; collecting and storing a vast number of books from pirated sources is another legal problem. The settlement therefore cannot be understood as a universal ruling that “using all books for AI training is illegal.” In Kadrey v. Meta, meanwhile, authors alleged that Meta had trained its models on books obtained from shadow libraries. The court found some force in the fair-use argument as it applied to the training process, while other claims remained unresolved.

These cases raise a larger question. A writer spends years working on a novel. A publisher brings it to market, and readers buy it. If the same book is then collected without permission and used to train a commercial AI model, does the writer have no rights to claim? Technology companies argue that models do not simply memorize the sentences in books; they learn statistical relationships and patterns in language. Writers respond that the material from which the model learns is itself the product of their creative labour. If a commercial technology is built on that labour, questions of authors’ rights and compensation cannot simply be avoided.

In my view, alongside the question of whether writers should be allowed to use AI, we should give equal importance to the question of how AI companies acquire the right to use writers’ work.

On July 24, 2026, the Delhi High Court in India made an important ruling in ANI Media Pvt. Ltd. v. OpenAI. The news agency ANI alleged that its copyrighted news reports and other writing had been used without permission to train ChatGPT. At that stage, the court declined to grant an interim injunction. In its preliminary view, the use of the material for model training might fall within the research-related exception under Indian copyright law. This was not a final determination of the case. The position in the United Kingdom is somewhat different. In 2025, the government considered proposals for exceptions covering the use of copyrighted works for AI training, along with an opt-out mechanism for authors. But a government report published on March 18, 2026, said that no new copyright reform would be introduced until the necessary evidence and economic impact had been established. In other words, the earlier proposed route was not being carried forward as a settled policy.

The European Union, meanwhile, has placed particular emphasis on transparency in AI use. Under Article 50 of the EU AI Act, obligations concerning the identifiability of certain AI-generated or altered content took effect on August 2, 2026. There are special provisions for literature, art, and creative works so that the enjoyment of artistic work is not unnecessarily disrupted. There are also separate rules for printed AI-generated material intended to communicate information in the public interest, along with exceptions involving human review and editorial control. European policy therefore should not be understood as a law banning AI from all literary work. These three examples show that the world has still not reached a common position on AI and copyright.

The 2026 Pulitzer Prize journalism guidelines state that the use of generative AI in submitted work should be disclosed. But these guidelines apply to journalism categories; they should not be treated as a universal prohibition across all literary categories. The 2026 Booker Prize rules set requirements concerning language, publication, and eligibility; there is no basis for concluding from them that every form of AI assistance is prohibited. The Authors Guild in the United States has introduced a “Human Authored Certification.” Its purpose is to help readers identify books whose core text was created by humans. In May 2026, the organization revised its definition. Under the revised definition, the text of the book must be entirely human-written, although very limited AI assistance, such as spelling and grammar checking, is acceptable. Publishers such as Elsevier are also emphasizing transparency, authorship, and human accountability in research and manuscripts; AI is not being recognized as an author. Taken together, a tendency is becoming clear internationally: rather than completely banishing AI, institutions are increasingly trying to establish ways of knowing how much AI was used, for what purpose, and at what stage of the work.

AI use can be divided into three levels. The first is assistive use: correcting spelling, identifying linguistic inconsistencies, producing a preliminary translation, finding historical information, explaining a difficult subject in simpler terms, or identifying weaknesses in one’s own writing. In such cases, creative decisions and responsibility remain with the writer. The second is collaborative use. A writer discusses a character’s psychology, asks for five possible versions of a scene, requests a counterargument to their own reasoning, or seeks advice about the structure of a chapter. AI brings forward new ideas and possibilities, but the writer decides what to accept, what to reject, and what the final form will be. The third is replacement use. The writer does almost none of the work of constructing the plot, characters, scenes, or language, but gives a few instructions, generates an entire novel, and publishes it under their own name. In the conventional sense, it is difficult to call this literary practice. The writer has handed over the very space of creative labour to a machine. In reality, however, there are many grey areas between these three levels. One writer may take an AI-generated paragraph, break it apart, and rebuild it in their own language. Another may have AI write the dialogue while creating the emotional movement and outcome of the scene themselves. In such cases, the measure should be the human creative contribution. My position is that using AI as assistance and passing AI-generated writing off as one’s own are not the same thing. The first can be a method of working. The second is a question of literary honesty.

A comparison comes to mind. A camera can take a photograph, but the camera itself is not the photographer. Nor can a photographer’s originality be denied simply because they used a camera. But if someone takes another person’s photograph and presents it as their own, that is plagiarism. The distinction with AI is similar. There is also an older truth worth remembering. The separation between a name and a hand did not begin with AI. In the age of the puthi in Bengal, scribes copied down the songs of poets, while the scribes’ own names were often forgotten. In world literature, many autobiographies were written by hired hands, while readers knew only the person named on the title page. There is one difference: those anonymous people were still human. They sweated, thought, and used their minds. AI is not human, and there is no person behind it from whom accountability can be demanded. The practice of lending a name is therefore old, but the question is new, and this time the question is much larger.

The example of Japanese writer Rie Kudan is worth mentioning here. In 2024, her novel Tokyo-to Dojo-to (Sympathy Tower Tokyo in English) won the Akutagawa Prize. After receiving the prize, she said that around five percent of the novel had been taken directly from ChatGPT, and that she had used some AI-generated sentences verbatim. Her admission sparked debate in Japan and in literary circles internationally. But Kudan did not have an entire novel written by AI and pass it off under her own name. She used machine-generated language as part of a literary experiment and openly acknowledged it. People may disagree about her method, but there is no reason to treat the use of AI and deception about authorship as the same thing.

American writer Sheila Heti’s “According to Alice,” published in The New Yorker in 2023, is another kind of experiment. She spoke with a chatbot, collected its answers, set aside her own questions, and built the story through editing and arrangement. Vauhini Vara’s Searches is another example of experimental writing about AI, personal memory, and the relationship between people and technology. These works suggest that AI can be considered not only a machine for writing stories but also a new literary medium.

There are precedents for embracing technology in the history of literature. In old age, Rabindranath Tagore sat in the studio of the Gramophone Company and recorded his own songs; many of Kazi Nazrul Islam’s songs were recorded on gramophone discs and reached homes across the country. Even then, some people grumbled that imprisoning a human voice inside a machine was an insult to art. Today those simple recordings are among the last traces of the voices of the two poets. When radio arrived, many writers feared that people would abandon books and sit in front of a box; when cinema arrived, playwrights feared the same thing. History has shown that each new medium did not destroy literature; it gave literature new forms. There is therefore no reason to see AI only as an enemy. But setting limits is harder than raising an alarm, and that is precisely what needs to be done.

Language-based AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini can be used for research, information analysis, character development, story structure, language editing, and literary criticism. There are also dedicated platforms for fiction writers, such as Sudowrite and Novelcrafter. The first can help expand scenes, describe characters, and suggest possible turns in a story. The second helps organize information about characters, places, and story elements. A historical novelist can use AI to research the social customs, administration, zamindari system, agriculture, waterways, clothing, or food habits of a particular period. But treating AI-generated information as final truth is dangerous. Historical facts, law, regional words, folk culture, and old documents are all areas where errors can occur. Writers must verify such information against primary sources, reliable scholarship, and historical records. The same is true of criticism. AI may point out where a description has become too long or where dialogue does not fit a character’s social position. But an AI critique is not necessarily correct; the writer is not obliged to agree with it. Perhaps the most effective use of AI is to test the writer’s own thinking. One can ask it to generate five possible endings, reject all five, and then discover a sixth ending oneself. In that process, AI is not an alternative to the writer but an additional field of thought.

There is so much discussion of AI in world literature, so much experimentation, so much litigation, and so many institutional policies being developed. Now let us look at the literary world of Bangladesh. Discussion of AI has begun here too, and its use in writing is growing. But we have no reliable national statistics showing how many writers use AI or how many books have been published with its assistance. There is therefore no basis for making numerical claims. But this country has its own realities, and it is difficult to take part in the AI debate without understanding them. Every February, thousands of new books arrive at the book fair, yet most writers in Bangladesh cannot support their households through writing income. In Facebook PDF groups with hundreds of thousands of members, books are uploaded day and night; people do not buy books, they simply search for files. The writer writes, the publisher invests, and the reader reads through piracy. Now AI joins that situation. A reader may not even need to read the whole book anymore; they can ask for a summary, or ask for a new draft “in the same style.” The pressure on the market for writers will grow. Foreign publishers are fighting legal battles, while here, as far as we know, we have not even seen a major court judgment concerning pirated PDFs. So before drawing international comparisons, it is important to keep the realities of our own home in view.

A study published in Rupkatha Journal on Interdisciplinary Studies in Humanities in 2024 does, however, offer some indications. It analyzed the views of six established writers and scholars and fifteen emerging writers. The study found that AI can help generate new ideas, organize the structure of writing, increase speed, and improve linguistic ability. But its responses are often formulaic and repetitive. Limitations in originality and emotional depth also emerged. The participating writers expressed concern that excessive dependence on AI could weaken the distinctiveness of their writing. This was not a national survey, and the number of participants was limited. Even so, it brings several important aspects of the AI debate in Bangladesh into view.

Whenever AI comes up in Bangladesh’s literary circles, a certain kind of resistance becomes visible. Some believe that using AI itself demeans authorship. Some think originality disappears the moment a writer accepts help from a machine. Others compare AI-generated writing directly with plagiarism. Not all of these objections are unreasonable. Publishing AI-generated writing under one’s own name, imitating another writer’s language and ideas, or using a writer’s work to train a model without permission all raise ethical and legal objections. The problem begins when every form of AI use is treated as the same thing. One writer may use AI to correct spelling, while another may give it a few instructions and produce an entire novel. Their work cannot reasonably be judged by the same moral standard.

There is another uncomfortable tendency worth mentioning. We often take a position against a new technology before we have understood it properly, especially among our older generation. Yet in the history of literature, every arrival—the printing press, newspapers, periodicals, radio, television, and the internet—created suspicion. In the end, literature used each medium for its own purposes. AI requires the same kind of caution. Rejecting a technology without understanding it is an intellectual narrowness; being dazzled by its capabilities and surrendering one’s own creative responsibility is self-deception.

A large part of our literature has still not been properly preserved in digital form. Old newspapers and magazines, regional literature, folklore, oral histories, rare books, and many works by important writers are not available in collections that can easily be searched. This is not merely a technological problem; it is also a problem of cultural preservation. Consider this: literature that was never printed in books at all—Lalon’s songs, the couplets of Bauls, pala songs, jari and sari songs—still remains, in a sense, invisible to machines. If the spoken languages of Barishal, Noakhali, Sylhet, Chattogram, Mymensingh, and northern Bangladesh, along with folk sayings, regional pronunciation, old words, and occupation-specific vocabulary, remain trapped behind the walls of standard prose, then a large part of our literary reality will remain invisible to AI. If the Bengali literary archive does not reach AI systems properly, future models will work with an incomplete understanding of the diversity and traditions of the Bengali language. In September 2026, The Daily Star brought the questions of Bengali literature and copyright to the fore in connection with Anthropic’s Project Panama. If digital collections of Bengali books are used for AI training in the future, we need to start discussing now how authors’ consent, publishers’ rights, and compensation will be determined. Digitizing the literary archive is urgent. But that does not mean anyone should be free to use a writer’s books commercially without permission. Preservation and protection of rights must proceed together.

One of the major weaknesses of the AI debate in Bangladesh is that we often declare a moral position about the technology without analyzing the nature of the particular use. One writer is looking for research information, another is preparing a translation draft, a third is discussing a character, and a fourth is generating an entire novel and publishing it under their own name. It is not reasonable to put all of them in the same category. People may object to AI. Choosing not to use it can be an individual and literary decision. But no one has the right to call another writer unfit or dishonest simply because that writer accepts assistance. At the same time, there is no justification for treating the publication of AI-generated writing under one’s own name as a legitimate expression of technological freedom. Literary people need reasoned discussion, publishers need to develop their own policies, and prize judges need to know how a writer’s creative contribution can be verified.

More important than opposing technology is setting limits on it. And to set those limits, we first need to understand clearly what the technology can do, what it cannot do, and which parts of a writer’s work should never be handed over to a machine.

It is difficult to say with certainty where AI’s role in literature will stand ten or fifteen years from now. But I suspect AI will not stop people from writing literature. Instead, the amount of writing will increase greatly, and the difference between good literature and the rest will become sharper. When a story can be produced in a few minutes, the important questions become: Which story needs to be written? Why does it need to be written? And what does it contain that can bring a reader closer to the life of another human being? AI may one day write novels with complex plots, convincing characters, and polished language; it may write poetry too. But literary quality does not end with beautiful language or skillful storytelling. What also matters is how a work captures its time, what unseen door of the human mind it opens, and how deeply it questions accepted truths. When technical mastery of language becomes readily available, a writer’s distinctiveness will have to be sought in thought, experience, observation, and the writer’s own way of seeing the world. For a historical novelist, the depth of research and fidelity to history will remain important; for a fiction writer, a personal understanding of the human mind and of life; for a poet, an individual use of language. A writer who brings personal experience, a sense of history, a philosophy of life, and imagination to the work will find opportunities to use AI to enrich it. A writer who relies only on familiar plots and beautiful sentences will face a much harder competition.

A writer can discuss things with AI, gather information from it, reject its ideas, and even learn something from it that had never occurred to them before. But in the end, a writer must have a world of their own. The language, experience, memory, and responsibility of that world cannot be handed over to someone—or something—else.

The biggest question of the future is not whether AI can truly write. The question will be how well a writer can preserve their own voice amid AI’s enormous command of language. A writer who draws upon personal experience, a sense of history, and imagination will not have their pen rendered unnecessary by any machine. If anything, readers’ expectations of such a writer will become greater. A machine can write a story, but it cannot write the reason why the story needed to be written. And that reason is, after all, what literature is.
